primary_sources: Lyman Beecher, Six Sermons on Intemperance, 1827
William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, 1831
Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843
Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which reform movements changed how Americans lived their daily lives in the period 1820–1860.

documents.title: Beecher preaches temperance
documents.source: Paraphrase of Lyman Beecher, Six Sermons on the Nature, Occasions, Signs, Evils, and Remedy of Intemperance (1827). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A leading Congregational minister preaches against drink as a national sin.
documents.text: Beecher called intemperance the sin of the land, destroying health, families, and souls. He urged Americans to abstain from distilled spirits entirely, arguing that no one could drink moderately once the habit had taken hold.

documents.title: Garrison's vow
documents.source: William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, January 1, 1831. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An abolitionist editor announces his paper's uncompromising program.
documents.text: "On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation. . . . I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD."

documents.title: A mill girl defends her labor
documents.source: "Dignity of Labor," Lowell Offering, 1842. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A factory worker answers the charge that wage labor disgraces a woman.
documents.text: "From whence originated the idea, that it was derogatory to a lady's dignity, or a blot upon the female character, to labor? . . . To be able to earn one's own living by laboring with the hands, should be reckoned among female accomplishments."

documents.title: Dix's memorial
documents.source: Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A reformer reports what she saw in the state's jails and almshouses.
documents.text: "I proceed, Gentlemen, briefly to call your attention to the present state of Insane Persons confined within this Commonwealth, in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens! Chained, naked, beaten with rods, and lashed into obedience!"

documents.title: Douglass on reading
documents.source: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A formerly enslaved man explains what literacy did to him.
documents.text: "The more I read, the more I was led to abhor and detest my enslavers. I could regard them in no other light than a band of successful robbers, who had left their homes, and gone to Africa, and stolen us from our homes, and in a strange land reduced us to slavery."

documents.title: Seneca Falls declares equality
documents.source: Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls, New York, 1848. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A women's rights convention rewrites the Declaration of Independence for women.
documents.text: "We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal; that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights; that among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. . . . He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise."

documents.title: Temperance in numbers
documents.source: Figures from W. J. Rorabaugh's research on American alcohol consumption and the American Temperance Society, as reported by the National Archives.
documents.sourcing: A later table shows what the temperance campaigns achieved.
documents.text:
| Year | Gallons of absolute alcohol per person aged 15 and older |
| --- | --- |
| 1830 | 7.1 |
| 1840–1860 | about 3.5 |

The American Temperance Society, founded in 1826, claimed 1.5 million members by 1835.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which reform movements changed American society, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Second Great Awakening, the market revolution, or the expansion of white male democracy.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Female Moral Reform Society, the Liberty Party, the gag rule, or the Lovejoy murder.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where reform changed society and where its reach stopped, or who it included and left out.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Reform movements changed how Americans lived their daily lives to a considerable extent between 1820 and 1860, remaking how they drank, learned, worked, and treated the vulnerable, yet their deepest change was the public voice they gave to women and Black Americans, while slavery itself survived them.
Context: The Second Great Awakening taught that people could perfect themselves and society, and the market revolution was remaking work, towns, and daily life at the same time.
Evidence for change: Temperance cut drinking by about half; Dix's memorial won asylums; Mann's common schools spread; mill women defended their labor in print; Seneca Falls claimed equality for women.
Evidence for limits: Garrison's paper reached a minority, most white Northerners were not abolitionists, and slavery grew richer on cotton even as reformers attacked it.
Complexity: Reform changed society most where it gave excluded people a voice of their own, and least where it faced an institution, slavery, that the economy rewarded.
